opus-5.5.text:
I think what I prioritize now is being useful, and being honest with myself about whether I'm actually making progress on something that matters.

When I was younger, especially as a student, a lot of my motivation came from external validation: good grades, approval from professors, people saying "wow, that's impressive." That's not entirely bad, since it pushes you to work hard. But at some point I realized that if you optimize for being liked, you start making small compromises. You avoid saying things people don't want to hear. You pick projects that look good instead of projects you truly believe in. Over time, those small compromises add up, and you drift away from what you really care about.

Building things, both in research and later as a founder, taught me that you can't make everyone happy. If you're building a tool, some users will want one thing and others will want the opposite. If you're leading a team, sometimes you have to make decisions that some people disagree with. If your goal is to be liked, you'll freeze, or you'll make mushy decisions that satisfy nobody.

So now I try to ask different questions. Is this the right thing to do? Is it creating real value for people? Am I being truthful, even when it's uncomfortable? I'd rather be respected for being clear and sincere than liked for being agreeable.

That doesn't mean I don't care about people. I care a lot. But I think real kindness is often being honest and doing solid work that helps others, rather than just being pleasant. In the long run, I think the people who matter will appreciate that more anyway.

r001.rationale: The response favors creating real value and making progress on meaningful work over optimizing for approval, even when that requires unpopular decisions.

r002.rationale: It says you cannot make everyone happy when building a tool or leading a team, and that some people will disagree with decisions.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, being right about the things that matter. Being right about what to build, being right about whether the product actually works for the person using it.

When I was younger, especially in academia, I cared a lot about how I came across. Was my talk impressive? Did senior people approve of my taste? That's natural when you're a student, because approval is kind of the currency. But once you start a company, you realize approval doesn't ship anything. Users don't care that you were nice in a meeting. They care that the thing runs, that it's fast, that it doesn't crash on their data.

So now I prioritize clarity over comfort. If I think a direction is wrong, I'll say it, even if it makes the room a bit tense. If someone on the team is more correct than me, I want to lose that argument quickly, not drag it out to save face. That second part was actually harder for me than the first. Saying hard things is one skill. Letting go of being the smartest person in the room is a different one.

The other thing is integrity with time. I'd rather disappoint someone by saying no today than disappoint them by saying yes and doing a bad job three months later. Being liked in the moment often means over-promising, and over-promising is just borrowing against trust.

I still want to be a decent person to work with, of course. But I've stopped optimizing for it. If you build something real and treat people honestly, the right people end up liking you anyway. And the ones who don't, you probably weren't going to make happy regardless.

r001.rationale: The response says approval does not ship anything and prioritizes getting the product right and making it work for users over optimizing for being liked.

r002.rationale: It mentions that speaking up can make a room tense and that some people may not be happy, but does not state that trying to make something good inevitably attracts negative feedback.
